extracted.intended_audience: general public; policymakers, emergency managers, and researchers interested in wildfire response/recovery
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic event report covering the 2018 Camp Fire: its causes, investigation, economic impacts, response, cleanup, recovery, and policy implications. The page collects findings, legal/regulatory actions, and reconstruction standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictors of water system contamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Density of structural loss was more predictive of water system contamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies indicated that calculating burn severity using satellite imagery were not appropriate for classifying localized burn severity within WUI communities; density of structural loss was a better predictor of contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price gouging prohibition (Chico emergency ordinance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit price gouging by preventing the cost of rent, goods or services from being increased by more than 10 percent for six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinance passed by Chico city council on November 16 (emergency measure after the Camp Fire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creditor priority in PG&E bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire survivors are unsecured creditors with the same priority as bondholders and will only be paid in proportion to their claim size after secured and priority claims are paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ordering of priorities nearly ensures unsecured wildfire victims will not be paid in full if funds are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility deadline for participation in California wildfire insurance fund
rubrics_metrics.description: PG&E had a deadline of June 30, 2020 to exit bankruptcy in order to participate in the California state wildfire insurance fund established by AB 1054.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exiting bankruptcy by the deadline was an eligibility requirement for utilities to access the state fund that helps pay for future wildfire claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement payment composition for wildfire victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Wildfire victims will get half of their $13.5 billion settlement as stock shares in the reorganized company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The stock component added uncertainty about when and how much victims would be paid; market impacts (e.g., COVID-19) affected decisions to increase the amount of stock or cash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable claim types to the Fire Victim Trust (FVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for wildfire victims include real estate and personal property, personal income loss, business loss, wrongful death, personal injury, emotional distress, zone of danger, and nuisance claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimants came from multiple prior wildfires (2015 Butte Fire, 2017 North Bay Fires, 2018 Camp Fire); certain other events (e.g., 2019 Kincade Fire) were not covered by the FVT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary payments policy (FVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: FVT began issuing Preliminary Payments up to $25,000 for those with significant losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary payments started November 23, 2020 to provide immediate relief before full claims processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro Rata Payments schedule (FVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial Pro Rata Payments were partial payments: the first installment was 30 percent of the Approved Claim Amount; later payments increased to a Pro Rata of 45 percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial payments reflected that the total amount available to the FVT was unknown; payment percentages adjusted over time as more funds were clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative process for determining cause and compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: State agencies (Cal Fire and state utility regulators) investigated PG&E to determine compliance with state laws and to identify ignition sources and equipment failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations included inspection of transmission/distribution lines, discovery of worn/broken components (e.g., a broken steel hook), review of prior incidents, and coordination with district attorneys and other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning system participation and delivery-performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Many residents did not sign up for emergency warnings and the failure rate of delivered warnings ranged from 25 to 94 percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance was hampered by damaged cell towers and insufficient cell-phone repeaters; remediation included adding mobile repeaters and commitments from telecom providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire response resource allocation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Resource mobilization measured by numbers of personnel and equipment (e.g., at peak 5,596 firefighters including 770 inmate firefighters; 622 engines; 75 water tenders; 101 fire crews; 103 bulldozers; aircraft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Camp Fire resource needs equaled the entirety of Cal Fire's full-time professionals and were stretched further because other large fires occurred concurrently; timing (high winds limited air support initially) affected deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evacuation sheltering and hygiene standards (post-event outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evacuation response included motel room vouchers and ten shelters; overcrowded centers experienced hygiene failures leading to norovirus outbreaks (100+ ill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large volunteer response supplemented services, but overcrowding and poor hygiene were identified as problems in shelter operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water monitoring sampling frequency and testing criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A months-long water monitoring program sampled surface water at least seven times through spring 2019 to assess contamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing focused on heavy metals, dioxins, benzene (from burning plastic pipes), and intestinal parasites such as cryptosporidium; initial testing of drinking systems (e.g., '22 out of 24 water systems were tested') was later revised when contamination was discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanup procurement and offhaul site selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Government procurement for cleanup was broken into several contract packages and put out to public bid to remove, process, and dispose of five million tons of materials; candidate sites were evaluated based on industrial zoning and presence of a rail spur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of fifty potential sites within thirty miles, some (e.g., Koppers Superfund Site) were dismissed over toxicity concerns; ultimately many materials were hauled long distances to approved landfills; several large contractor awards (with contract values) were listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline requirement for salvage logging
rubrics_metrics.description: Salvage logging of 443,000 dead trees must be done within a few months or the trees will begin to rot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradise Fire Safe Council considered bids and pilot programs to test feasibility; delays complicate salvage value and hazard mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment criteria for appropriateness of residential development in wildland–urban interface
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions whether to allow development hinge on whether development can be made safe and, if so, what building codes and emergency-response infrastructure would be needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographic features (proximity/alignment to river canyons that channel wind-fed flames) and local fire-mapping tiers were cited as factors that make some areas unsuitable for subdivision development.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPUC Fire-Threat Map tiering
rubrics_metrics.description: The CPUC Fire-Threat Map classifies regions into tiers such as Tier 2 (elevated hazard) and Tier 3 (extreme hazard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tier mapping was referenced as part of regulatory action and informed post-Camp Fire policy changes (e.g., rules for disabling power lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules governing pre-emptive power shutoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory rules were revised to improve guidelines on when utilities should disable power lines to reduce wildfire risk (public utilities commission action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CPUC voted December 15, 2018 to improve rules; these measures seek to balance risk reduction against impacts like outages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for prioritizing electrical infrastructure hardening
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardening options include undergrounding distribution (reduces spark risk but increases cost by ~10x) and selectively hardening high-energy lines through high-wind areas upwind of residential communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers must weigh cost constraints (e.g., 10x cost to bury lines) and prioritize locations (e.g., river canyon approaches to communities); legislative and pilot programs inform implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuilding standards for fire-resistant construction and infrastructure upgrades
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuilding promoted with higher standards for fire-resistant construction, upgraded infrastructure, and use of recommended redesigns for enhanced fire safety (including expanded road capacity to increase evacuation capacity and to provide better access for emergency equipment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local policymakers encouraged these standards; first building permits were reissued after ~five months and Certificates of Occupancy resumed (first awarded July 2019).
